content.value: Read method headers; match arguments to parameters; distinguish return types, method names, and overloads.

A method header declares an operation. Its return type indicates the kind of result, or void when no value is returned. The method name and parameter types identify how callers invoke it. A parameter is a variable in the declaration; an argument is a value or expression at the call site. Arguments match parameters by position, not by the caller’s variable names.

Overloaded methods share a name but differ in parameter lists. Changing only the return type or parameter names does not create a valid distinct overload. Java checks the number of arguments and compatible types; some widening conversions such as int to double are permitted.

first receives 10 and second receives 3, so result is 7. Reversing the arguments produces -7. The header specifies two int parameters and an int result; neither the access modifier nor the method name is the return type.
Calling difference(10) omits a required argument. difference("10", 3) supplies an incompatible String. A void method can perform actions but cannot appear where a value is required.

Write the call to difference that returns 12 from inputs 20 and 8. Then propose a distinct overload with two double parameters. Explain why changing only the parameter names does not produce an overload.
